lines: An engineer wants to rename a column that half the pipeline has quietly been calling by one particular name for years.

The catalog's own index says a small handful of tables actually read it. How many owners genuinely need to hear about this before it ships — and how many will still be missed, even if the lineage behind it works exactly as designed?
So which of these numbers do you actually trust here?
The catalog's own count, a full graph walk's count — or is neither one, on its own, the real answer to who should be told before this change goes out? Sit with that for a second before I go on.
answer: Neither one alone gets you there. A static catalog only knows what it was told directly, so it tends to undercount by a wide margin.
A full graph walk finds everyone downstream, which is genuinely more complete — but it also drags in some tables that never actually touch the column in question at all.

lines: So, start at the table the renamed column actually lives in, and follow every single edge downstream from there.

Any number of hops, and it doesn't matter yet which particular column is carrying the data forward — on the real run just done here, that walk turns up far more consumers than the catalog's static list ever had on record.

Now narrow it. Follow only the edges where that specific column actually keeps propagating, tracked straight through every rename along the way — whether it's copied over directly or just shapes a downstream value without appearing by name.
On that exact same graph, this narrower walk excludes a few specific, named tables the broader walk had wrongly pulled in — tables that, it turns out, never touched this column at all.
steps.takeaway: Table-level lineage finds who's downstream; column-level lineage finds who actually reads the thing changing.

lines: Blast radius is one question. A run failing outright turns out to be a genuinely different one.

When the whole partition goes bad, every column in it becomes suspect, not just the one somebody happened to be tracking — so staleness has to spread along the full table-level graph, not the narrower column-level one.
On the real run here, that marks every single table-level dependent stale, full stop.
steps.takeaway: Blast radius and stale propagation ask different questions, so they walk the graph differently.

lines: Here's the step that actually keeps this usable at scale: resolve every affected table back to whoever owns it, and send exactly one message per owner, listing everything of theirs that's touched.
On the real run here, a double-digit number of affected tables collapses down into just a small handful of notifications — nobody on this list hears the same news twice.
steps.takeaway: Deduplicating by owner, not by table, is what keeps one incident from flooding an inbox.

lines: A table that still has live dependents simply can't be pulled out from under them.
On the real run here, trying to deprecate a table while dependents are still outstanding gets refused outright — and the refusal names, specifically, exactly which owners still haven't signed off.
Now flip it: once every one of those dependent owners has actually signed off — or a table never had any dependents to begin with — that same workflow goes ahead and proceeds.

Both of those cases run for real, on the exact same graph: a table with no dependents deprecates immediately, while the dependent-heavy one only goes through once every last sign-off has actually landed.
So, gathering all of this together.
Six different pieces, all working together here. A static index misses people. A full graph walk pulls in too many, by name. Narrowing to the column alone gets it right.

A bad partition doesn't care which single value somebody cared about — it taints the whole row. Each person hears from this exactly once. And nothing gets retired until every last signature is actually in.
One more case, worth sitting with for a moment.
Somewhere, a table gets read by name, straight out of a script that never once calls the lineage API.

As the rest of this graph's coverage keeps getting better and better over time, will blast-radius scoring, stale propagation, or owner notification ever actually catch sight of that particular reader? And why, or why not?
answer: Never — not from this particular gap, anyway. Every one of these methods only walks edges that already exist somewhere in the graph.
A reader that never reports a single run leaves no edge behind for any of them to follow, no matter how complete the rest of the graph eventually becomes.
